title: Immunovaccine Technologies Inc. (Sept 2014 FCA) Ruling
subject: Federal Court of Appeal case on whether provincial government assistance reduced qualified SR&ED expenditures.
summary: Immunovaccine Technologies Inc. v. Her Majesty the Queen, 2014 FCA 196, is a Federal Court of Appeal decision for Canadian SR&ED claimants receiving public funding. The Court held that a $3,786,474 conditionally repayable ACOA contribution was "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, reducing claimable SR&ED expenditures and refundable investment tax credits for 2005 to 2008.
metaDescription: Analyze the September 2014 Federal Court of Appeal ruling for Immunovaccine Technologies Inc. on Canadian SR&ED tax credits.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary and Case Background
Factual Matrix and the Taxpayer's Claim

The decision of the Federal Court of Appeal ("FCA") in Immunovaccine Technologies Inc. v. Her Majesty the Queen, 2014 FCA 196 (Docket A-171-13), delivered on September 11, 2014, stands as a foundational authority in Canadian tax jurisprudence governing the intersection of public-sector innovation funding and Scientific Research and Experimental Development ("SR&ED") tax incentives. The appellant, Immunovaccine Technologies Inc. ("Immunovaccine"), is a Canadian biotechnology company based in Halifax, Nova Scotia, engaged in the research and development of vaccines against infectious diseases.

To finance its research operations, Immunovaccine entered into a contribution agreement on December 31, 2004 ("the Agreement") with the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency ("ACOA"), a federal Crown agency established under the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. 41 (4th Supp.), whose statutory mandate is to support and promote economic development across the Atlantic region of Canada. Under the Agreement—administered through ACOA's Atlantic Innovation Fund ("AIF")—ACOA committed nearly $3.8 million in financial support over four consecutive taxation years spanning 2005 through 2008. Pursuant to the Agreement, Immunovaccine received aggregate disbursements of $3,786,474 between 2005 and 2008.

In filing its T2 corporate income tax returns and prescribed SR&ED schedules (Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31) for the 2005, 2006, 2007, and 2008 taxation years, Immunovaccine claimed SR&ED deductible expenditure pools under subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) ("ITA") and claimed corresponding Refundable Investment Tax Credits ("RITCs") pursuant to subsections 127(5), 127(9), and 127.1(1) of the ITA. Immunovaccine took the filing position that the $3,786,474 received from ACOA did not reduce its qualified SR&ED expenditures because the Agreement required repayment of the principal contribution out of future gross revenues. Consequently, the taxpayer characterized the ACOA advances as a commercial "regular loan" rather than a "forgivable loan" or other form of "government assistance" defined under subsection 127(9) of the ITA.
The Minister's Challenge and Procedural History

By determinations dated March 14, 2008 (2005 and 2006 taxation years) and July 15, 2009 (2007 and 2008 taxation years), the Minister of National Revenue ("the Minister"), acting through the Canada Revenue Agency ("CRA"), dealt with the ACOA payments relating to the 2005, 2006, 2007, and 2008 taxation years. The Minister determined that the $3,786,474 received from ACOA constituted "government assistance" within the meaning of subsection 127(9) of the ITA. Because government assistance directly reduces both the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(d) and "qualified expenditures" under subsection 127(18), the Minister denied Immunovaccine's SR&ED expenditure claims to the extent of the ACOA funding and disallowed its entitlement to RITCs under subsection 127.1(1) for each of the four taxation years.

Immunovaccine appealed the Minister's determinations to the Tax Court of Canada ("TCC"). On April 10, 2013, in Immunovaccine Technologies Inc. v. The Queen, 2013 TCC 103 (Docket 2011-245(IT)G), Justice Lucie Lamarre dismissed the taxpayer's appeal. Justice Lamarre held that ACOA, in executing the Agreement, was fulfilling its statutory object and exercising its public powers under the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act. Based on the evidentiary record and contractual context, the TCC concluded that the ACOA contribution was "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) and was not a regular loan advanced on reasonable commercial terms for business purposes.

Immunovaccine appealed the TCC judgment to the Federal Court of Appeal, where the matter was heard in Halifax, Nova Scotia, on September 9, 2014, before a panel comprising Justices Nadon, Trudel, and Boivin. On September 11, 2014, the FCA unanimously dismissed the appeal with costs, with Justice Richard Boivin delivering the reasons for judgment. Immunovaccine subsequently sought leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada (Docket 36177), which dismissed the leave application with costs on March 26, 2015, rendering the FCA's judgment final and binding across Canada.
Governing Statutory and Regulatory Framework

The Canadian SR&ED tax incentive program operates through a dual-mechanism statutory architecture within the ITA: first, the pooling and current deduction of eligible R&D expenditures under section 37; and second, the generation of Investment Tax Credits ("ITCs") and RITCs on "qualified expenditures" under sections 127 and 127.1. A cardinal legislative principle underlying this regime is that tax incentives are intended to subsidize only the net, out-of-pocket economic cost borne by the taxpayer in performing SR&ED in Canada.

To prevent double-dipping—whereby a corporation finances its R&D using public grants or subsidies while simultaneously claiming SR&ED tax deductions and tax credits on those same gross outlays—Parliament enacted a comprehensive "assistance grind" across sections 12, 37, and 127 of the ITA.

cells: Subsection 127(9) ("government assistance")

Defines "government assistance" as assistance from a government, municipality, or other public authority whether as a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, investment allowance, or as any other form of assistance, other than as a deduction under subsection 127(5) or 127(6). For loans made after December 31, 2019, the definition also excludes an "excluded loan" as defined in subsection 12(11) (S.C. 2024, c. 17), and it now excludes deemed payments on account of tax under subsections 127.44(2), 127.45(2), 127.48(2), 127.49(2) and 127.491(2).
Establishes the threshold classification trigger; if funding falls within this definition, mandatory pool and expenditure reductions apply immediately.
Paragraph 37(1)(a) & Paragraph 37(1)(d)

Paragraph 37(1)(a) adds current SR&ED expenditures to the deductible SR&ED expenditure pool. Paragraph 37(1)(d) reduces the pool by any government or non-government assistance the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive in respect of SR&ED.
Diminishes the available tax deduction pool on an accrual basis at the filing-due date; if reductions create a negative pool balance, paragraph 12(1)(v) forces an immediate income inclusion.
Subsection 127(18) & Paragraph (h) of the "Qualified Expenditure" Definition in Subsection 127(9)

Reduces a taxpayer's "qualified expenditures" ("QEs") for a taxation year by the amount of government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payments received, entitled to be received, or reasonably expected to be received on or before the filing-due date in respect of the SR&ED project.
Directly reduces the expenditure base upon which the 15% basic ITC or 35% enhanced Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation ("CCPC") ITC is calculated, reducing or eliminating credit generation.
Subsections 127(19) & 127(20)

Governs project-level excess assistance and non-arm's length ("NAL") group allocations. Under subsection 127(19), excess assistance that the recipient's own QEs cannot absorb reduces the QEs of NAL persons for SR&ED performed while not dealing at arm's length with the recipient. Where subsection 127(19) does not apply, subsection 127(20) allows the parties to allocate the excess by an agreement filed on prescribed Form T1145; absent an agreement, subsection 127(21) deems the unallocated amount to be government assistance received by the NAL person.
Can wipe out QEs across related corporate entities to nil if government assistance exceeds single-entity project costs.
Subsection 127.1(1)
Provides for the refundability of unused ITCs earned in the year by qualifying CCPCs (and eligible capital/current shares) as Refundable Investment Tax Credits ("RITCs").
Denial of QEs under s. 127(18) eliminates the underlying ITC, directly stripping the corporation of non-dilutive cash refunds under s. 127.1(1).
Paragraph 37(1)(c) & Subsections 127(10.7) and 127(10.8)

Restores the SR&ED deductible pool (s. 37(1)(c)) and generates ITC additions (s. 127(10.7) and paragraphs (e.1)/(e.2) of the "investment tax credit" definition in s. 127(9)) solely in the subsequent taxation year in which government assistance is actually repaid or is deemed repaid under s. 127(10.8) because it has ceased to be reasonably expected to be received.
Defers tax relief to future years when cash repayments occur, creating a severe multi-year working capital deficit during the pre-revenue R&D phase.
Subparagraphs 12(1)(x)(iii) & (iv)

Includes in business income any inducement, reimbursement, contribution, or government assistance received in the year, to the extent it did not already reduce an expenditure pool under s. 37(1)(d) or capital cost under s. 13(7.1), subject to an expense-reduction election under s. 12(2.2).
Taxes excess or non-SR&ED government assistance as ordinary corporate income in the year of receipt unless properly structured or elected.

body.text: The Federal Court of Appeal's Final Holding and Broader Trajectory

The Federal Court of Appeal affirmed the TCC's judgment in its entirety, holding that the $3,786,474 advanced by ACOA constituted "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) of the ITA. Writing for the unanimous panel, Justice Boivin established three core legal propositions that govern the characterization of public-sector R&D funding. First, the statutory definition of "government assistance" in subsection 127(9) is intentionally broad; because the general term "assistance from a government" precedes the specific enumeration and the catch-all phrase "or as any other form of assistance" immediately follows it, the ejusdem generis rule of statutory construction cannot be invoked to limit the provision to purely gratuitous, unilateral grants or formally designated "forgivable loans". Second, the governing legal standard for distinguishing commercial transactions from "government assistance" remains the test articulated in Canada v. CCLC Technologies Inc., [1996] 3 C.T.C. 246, 96 D.T.C. 6527 (FCA) ("CCLC Technologies"), which asks whether the public authority made the payment in a business capacity—specifically, "in exactly the same way for exactly the same reasons as payments made by private business, that is, for the purpose of advancing the [business] interests of the payor". Third, the FCA agreed with the TCC that the language of the Agreement indicated the parties' intention to treat the contribution as government assistance and not as an ordinary business arrangement, pointing to several substantive provisions: the Agreement contains reporting requirements; repayment is required only to the extent and as a percentage of gross income earned; the Agreement ends in 2017 whether or not there has been repayment; and the most ACOA can expect is the return of its contribution without interest. On that basis, the contribution was properly characterized as "government assistance".

The doctrinal ripple effects of Immunovaccine across Canadian tax law have been profound. By cementing the CCLC Technologies commercial venture standard and rejecting narrow textualist exclusions for repayable contributions, Immunovaccine directly enabled the Crown's subsequent victory in CAE Inc. v. The Queen, 2021 TCC 57 (affirmed in CAE Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 178; leave to appeal to the SCC refused May 25, 2023). In CAE, the courts extended the Immunovaccine framework to hold that even an unconditionally repayable, interest-bearing government loan under Industry Canada's Strategic Aerospace and Defence Initiative ("SADI") constituted "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) and subparagraph 12(1)(x)(iv) because the Tax Court found that the loan's implicit rate of return was significantly lower than the market rate of return for a comparable loan and therefore contrary to the business interests of a private lender.

Although Parliament subsequently enacted legislative exceptions to protect bona fide, unconditional government loans with reasonable repayment terms (the "excluded loan" definition in subsection 12(11) of the ITA, added by the Budget Implementation Act, 2024, No. 1, S.C. 2024, c. 17, assented to June 20, 2024, and applicable to loans made after December 31, 2019) (particularly to prevent the clawback of clean energy and green technology investment tax credits following CAE), conditionally repayable contributions of the kind adjudicated in Immunovaccine remain fully subject to the subsection 127(18) and paragraph 37(1)(d) assistance grind. Furthermore, with the restoration of SR&ED capital expenditure eligibility effective December 16, 2024, and comprehensive SR&ED legislative enhancements receiving Royal Assent on March 26, 2026 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), proactive structuring around Immunovaccine remains a paramount concern for Canadian R&D tax advisors.
2. Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures
Contextualizing the Disqualification: Funded Research Exclusions Versus Scientific Eligibility

In Canadian SR&ED tax litigation, disputes generally bifurcate into two distinct categories: technical eligibility disputes under subsection 248(1) of the ITA (assessing whether the work involved technological uncertainty, specific hypotheses, a systematic process of experimentation, technological advancement, and contemporaneous documentation), and financial quantification disputes under sections 37 and 127 (assessing whether eligible expenditures are disqualified or reduced by funded research exclusions, government assistance, or contract payments).

In Immunovaccine, the technical eligibility of the appellant's scientific work developing infectious disease vaccines under subsection 248(1) was not at issue before the FCA; the only question decided was whether the ACOA payments constituted government assistance under subsection 127(9). Instead, the Minister's denial of Immunovaccine's SR&ED claims and RITCs for the 2005–2008 taxation years stemmed from the characterization of the ACOA payments as government assistance under subsection 127(9), which, as the FCA stated, reduces the amount of SR&ED expenses the appellant can claim for those years (through the mechanisms of paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18)). However, from a technical tax advisory perspective, Immunovaccine's disqualification exposed a dual failure: first, a legal and contractual failure to structure the ACOA financing as a commercial debt instrument; and second, a potential project governance and documentation issue, since the decision does not indicate whether ACOA-funded activities were segregated from self-funded SR&ED projects; the FCA records only that the ACOA sums reduce the amount of SR&ED expenses Immunovaccine could claim for the four years, and does not state that its entire SR&ED expenditure pool was eliminated.
Statutory Interpretation Failure: Misapplication of the Ejusdem Generis Canon to Subsection 127(9)

The centerpiece of Immunovaccine's appellate strategy before the FCA was an attempt to bypass established judicial precedent through a narrow textual interpretation of subsection 127(9) of the ITA. Before the FCA, counsel for Immunovaccine conceded that the test formulated in CCLC Technologies had been adopted by Canadian courts to determine whether public-sector payments constitute "government assistance". However, the appellant argued that it did not need to satisfy the CCLC Technologies test because that standard was merely a "judge-made-rule" that could not override the plain text of the statute.

Specifically, Immunovaccine contended that the ACOA Agreement was a repayable loan rather than a "forgivable loan," and invoked the ejusdem generis ("of the same kind or class") canon of statutory interpretation to restrict the scope of subsection 127(9). Subsection 127(9) defines "government assistance" as follows:

"government assistance" means assistance from a government, municipality or other public authority whether as a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, investment allowance or as any other form of assistance other than as a deduction under subsection 127(5) or 127(6).

Immunovaccine argued that the specific enumerated terms—grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, investment allowance—established a genus of purely gratuitous, unilateral financial transfers where the recipient has no obligation to repay the principal. Under the ejusdem generis rule, the appellant asserted that the trailing general phrase "or as any other form of assistance" must be confined to items of that exact same non-repayable genus, thereby excluding any bilateral loan agreement containing repayment covenants.

Justice Boivin dismantled this statutory interpretation argument at paragraphs 13 through 15 of the decision. The FCA did not set out general conditions for the application of the ejusdem generis canon; rather, it rejected the appellant's proposed textual interpretation by examining the wording of subsection 127(9) itself. In subsection 127(9), the FCA noted that the phrase "assistance from a government" precedes an enumeration (grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, investment allowance), while the words "or as any other form of assistance" immediately follow this enumeration.

Justice Boivin agreed with Justice Lamarre's conclusion at paragraph 45 of the TCC reasons that this statutory phrasing does not restrict the forms of assistance captured by subsection 127(9). Instead, the FCA held that such phrasing provides a broad meaning to the word "assistance," capable of encompassing a variety of forms of government assistance not necessarily limited to the enumeration, so that the definition can include agreements which are not purely gratuitous and unilateral.
Evidentiary Failure Under the CCLC Technologies Commercial Venture Test

Having rejected the appellant's ejusdem generis argument, the FCA reaffirmed that the authoritative legal framework for evaluating public-sector payments under subsection 127(9) is the line of jurisprudence culminating in CCLC Technologies, including Canada v. Consumers' Gas Co., [1987] 2 F.C. 60, [1987] 1 C.T.C. 79 (FCA) ("Consumers' Gas"), and Ottawa Valley Power Co. v. Minister of National Revenue, [1969] 2 Ex.C.R. 64, 69 D.T.C. 5166, confirmed on appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada at [1970] S.C.R. 941, [1970] C.T.C. 305. This jurisprudence is further reinforced in the SR&ED context by Radio Engineering Products Limited v. Minister of National Revenue, 73 D.T.C. 5071 (FCTD).

Under Consumers' Gas and CCLC Technologies, a payment made by a public authority pursuant to a contract escapes classification as "government assistance" only if the transaction exhibits the genuine attributes of an ordinary commercial venture—meaning the public authority is acting in a private business capacity rather than a public governance or policy capacity. As articulated by the FCA in CCLC Technologies and applied in Immunovaccine, the decisive legal question is whether the government payments were made:
"...in exactly the same way for exactly the same reasons as payments made by private business, that is, for the purpose of advancing the [business] interests of the payor."

Immunovaccine did not convince the FCA that the Tax Court judge committed a reviewable error in applying this standard. The FCA decision does not describe any commercial objective pursued by ACOA in advancing the funds to Immunovaccine. Rather, Justice Lamarre found—and the FCA, detecting no reviewable error, left undisturbed—that ACOA, in entering into the Agreement, was carrying out its object and exercising its powers under the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act, ACOA being a federal agency established to support the economic development of the Atlantic region. Under the CCLC Technologies test as applied by the FCA, where the public authority acts in a governance rather than a business capacity, its payments lack the attributes of a commercial venture and constitute "government assistance".
Contractual and Structural Deficiencies in the ACOA Agreement

To substantiate its contention that the ACOA funding was a "regular loan," Immunovaccine had to demonstrate that the terms of the December 31, 2004 Agreement established an ordinary commercial debtor-creditor relationship. Both the TCC and the FCA scrutinized the clauses of the Agreement and identified four fatal contractual deficiencies that refuted any characterization of the advances as a commercial loan. First, the Agreement contained reporting requirements; the decision identifies their existence as a factor but does not describe their specific content or purpose. Second, Immunovaccine was required to pay the contribution, but only to the extent and as a percentage of gross income earned; the decision does not describe a fixed repayment schedule or specify the source of that gross income. As noted in the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy reflecting this jurisprudence, the absence of firm, unconditional repayment terms—where repayment is contingent upon achieving future revenue thresholds—is a primary indicator that an advance is assistance rather than a genuine loan.

Third, the Agreement contained a fatal 2017 contractual sunset clause stipulating that the contract and all repayment obligations thereunder expired in 2017, regardless of whether Immunovaccine had repaid the full $3,786,474 contribution by that date. Because vaccine development in the biotechnology sector involves protracted preclinical and clinical trial timelines, this 2017 sunset clause operated as a built-in conditional forgiveness mechanism: if gross revenues did not reach levels sufficient to amortize the principal before 2017, the remaining balance was permanently extinguished. Fourth, the Agreement stipulated that the maximum amount ACOA could ever recover was the nominal return of its initial capital contribution without interest. In an arm's length commercial capital market, no private lender or venture debt provider would advance $3.8 million for high-risk, early-stage infectious disease vaccine R&D on a revenue-contingent basis where the best-case return is 0% nominal interest (representing a guaranteed real economic loss after accounting for inflation, time value of money, and default risk) and the worst-case return is total principal forfeiture in 2017.
Project Accounting and Timing Deficiencies: Accrual Recognition Versus Deferred Recapture

A critical structural failure highlighted by the Immunovaccine dispute lies in the asymmetric timing mechanics of the ITA regarding government assistance recognition versus repayment recapture. Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18), government assistance reduces the SR&ED expenditure pool and qualified expenditures in the taxation year in which the assistance is "received, is entitled to be received, or can reasonably be expected to be received" on or before the taxpayer's filing-due date.

The FCA decision states that, as government assistance, the sums Immunovaccine received from ACOA for the 2005–2008 tax years reduce the amount of SR&ED expenses it can claim for those years; it does not discuss whether the ACOA funds were segregated into non-SR&ED budget categories (such as commercial business development, market studies, or non-SR&ED clinical/regulatory activities) or how the in-respect-of requirement of subsection 127(18) applied to them. Consistent with that holding, the existence of a repayment obligation conditioned on gross income did not prevent the ACOA payments from being characterized as government assistance for the 2005, 2006, 2007, and 2008 tax years.

While paragraph 37(1)(c), paragraph (e.1) of the "investment tax credit" definition in subsection 127(9) and subsection 127(10.7) permit a taxpayer to restore its SR&ED pool and recover lost ITCs when government assistance is subsequently repaid, that relief is strictly deferred until the future taxation year in which actual cash repayments are made. For an early-stage biotechnology company requiring immediate RITC cash refunds under subsection 127.1(1) to fund laboratory operations during 2005–2008, the reduction of claimable SR&ED expenditures, and the corresponding denial of RITCs, can create a significant working capital shortfall during pre-revenue years, although the FCA decision itself does not address Immunovaccine's financial position or the quantum of credits affected.
Appellate Standard of Review: The Palpable and Overriding Error Barrier

Finally, Immunovaccine's appellate challenge faltered on the procedural standard of review governing tax appeals in Canada. Citing the Supreme Court of Canada's landmark decision in Housen v. Nikolaisen, 2002 SCC 33, [2002] 2 S.C.R. 235, Justice Boivin emphasized at paragraph 8 that findings of fact and questions of mixed fact and law made by a Tax Court judge are reviewable only under the highly deferential standard of "palpable and overriding error".

The FCA rejected the appellant's proposed ejusdem generis interpretation of subsection 127(9), noted that Justice Lamarre had referred to and applied the CCLC Technologies test, and agreed with her that the language of the Agreement indicated an intention to treat the contribution as government assistance rather than an ordinary business arrangement. Stating that it could not detect any error in the Judge's interpretation of the Agreement and that the appellant had not convinced it that the Judge committed a reviewable error warranting intervention, the FCA dismissed the appeal with costs.
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and jurisprudential requirement examined in Immunovaccine Technologies Inc. v. Her Majesty the Queen (2014 FCA 196) against the taxpayer's specific legal or evidentiary failure and the governing standard of proof established by the Court.

headers: Court's Standard of Proof & Final Holding

cells: Statutory Scope of "Government Assistance" (ITA, Subsection 127(9))

Argued via the ejusdem generis rule that the specific list (grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, investment allowance) restricted the trailing phrase "or as any other form of assistance" to unilateral, gratuitous, non-repayable transfers.

Broad & Purposive Textual Standard: Because "assistance from a government" precedes the enumeration and "or as any other form of assistance" follows it, the definition provides a broad meaning to "assistance," not necessarily limited to the enumeration, and can include agreements which are not purely gratuitous and unilateral.
Commercial Venture vs. Public Policy Mandate (CCLC Technologies, 96 D.T.C. 6527; Consumers' Gas, [1987] 2 F.C. 60; Ottawa Valley Power, [1970] S.C.R. 941)

Claimed the CCLC Technologies test was merely a "judge-made-rule" that need not be satisfied, and did not persuade the FCA that the Judge erred in finding that ACOA was carrying out its object and exercising its powers under the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act.

Ordinary Business Relationship Standard: The taxpayer must prove the public authority paid the funds "in exactly the same way for exactly the same reasons as payments made by private business" to advance the payor's business interests. ACOA acted under a public economic development statute, not as a commercial lender.
Unconditional Debt vs. Conditional Contribution (ITA, Subsection 127(9); Radio Engineering Products, 73 D.T.C. 5071)

Characterized the ACOA Agreement as a "regular loan" outside subsection 127(9) relying on the fact that the Agreement required repayment of the contribution (to the extent and as a percentage of gross income earned).

Contractual Language and Intention Standard: A genuine loan requires firm, unconditional repayment obligations. The FCA cited the requirement to repay the contribution only to the extent and as a percentage of gross income earned as one of several provisions indicating that the parties intended the contribution to be government assistance rather than an ordinary business arrangement.
Absence of De Facto Forgiveness / Sunset Clauses (ITA, Subsection 127(9) — "forgivable loan" or "any other form of assistance")
Asserted the advance was not a "forgivable loan", contending instead that the Agreement constituted a "regular loan" outside the subsection 127(9) definition.

Agreement Expiry Factor: The Agreement expired in 2017 regardless of whether the $3,786,474 had been repaid. The FCA listed this provision among the substantive provisions indicating that the parties intended the contribution to be government assistance rather than an ordinary business arrangement.
Market-Rate Return & Risk-Adjusted Consideration (CCLC Technologies, 96 D.T.C. 6527; Immunovaccine, 2014 FCA 196, para. 16)
Accepted $3,786,474 in high-risk biotechnology funding under terms where the maximum possible repayment to ACOA was the nominal principal without interest.

Commercial Return Standard: The FCA noted that the most ACOA could expect was the return of its contribution without interest, one of the provisions indicating government assistance rather than an ordinary business arrangement; the TCC had concluded that the contribution was not a regular loan advanced on reasonable terms for business purposes.
Covenant Structure & Reporting Obligations (Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. 41 (4th Supp.))
Entered into an ACOA Agreement containing reporting requirements.

Contractual Context Standard: The FCA listed the Agreement's reporting requirements among the substantive provisions indicating that the parties intended the contribution to be government assistance rather than an ordinary business arrangement; the decision does not describe the content of those requirements.
Expenditure Pool & QE Reduction ("In Respect Of" SR&ED) (ITA, Paragraph 37(1)(d), Subsection 127(18), & Subsection 127.1(1))
Treated the ACOA payments as a regular loan that did not reduce its SR&ED expenditures, claiming SR&ED deductions and RITCs for 2005–2008.

Accrual Reduction Standard: Government assistance received, entitled to be received, or reasonably expected to be received in respect of SR&ED automatically reduces the s. 37(1) pool and s. 127(18) QEs in the year of accrual (as the FCA confirmed, the ACOA sums reduce the amount of SR&ED expenses the appellant can claim), reducing RITC entitlement under s. 127.1(1) until actual repayment occurs under s. 37(1)(c) and s. 127(10.7).
Appellate Review of Contractual Characterization (Housen v. Nikolaisen, 2002 SCC 33)
Argued that the Judge erred in law in interpreting "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) and in applying that interpretation to the ACOA Agreement.

Palpable and Overriding Error Standard: Findings of fact and of mixed fact and law are reviewable for palpable and overriding error (Housen v. Nikolaisen); the FCA rejected the appellant's interpretation of subsection 127(9), detected no error in the Judge's interpretation of the Agreement, and dismissed the appeal with costs.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To demonstrate how Canadian corporate taxpayers and their advisors can proactively overcome the legal, contractual, technical, and accounting pitfalls identified in Immunovaccine (2014 FCA 196) and its subsequent judicial extension in CAE (2022 FCA 178), the following two industry case studies set out comprehensive, step-by-step remediation blueprints.
Case Study 1: Biopharmaceutical Adjuvant and mRNA Delivery Platform (Overcoming Conditional Contribution Contamination and Project Commingling)
Factual Scenario and Initial Legal Pitfalls

NovaVaxion BioLabs Inc. ("NovaVaxion") is a Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation ("CCPC") headquartered in Halifax, Nova Scotia, developing a proprietary thermostable lipid-nanoparticle ("LNP") mucosal vaccine platform. For its 2026–2028 fiscal cycle, NovaVaxion plans to spend $8,000,000 across two overarching corporate initiatives. The first initiative ("Initiative A") represents $4,000,000 in core bench-scale SR&ED aimed at resolving fundamental technological uncertainties regarding cationic lipid oxidation and antigen degradation at ambient temperatures (25°C to 40°C), which qualifies as eligible SR&ED under subsection 248(1) of the ITA. The second initiative ("Initiative B") represents $4,000,000 in non-SR&ED clinical, regulatory, and commercial scale-up work, comprising routine cGMP contract manufacturing of Phase I/II clinical trial batches, standard regulatory toxicology filings for Health Canada, and commercial packaging line commissioning—activities expressly excluded from SR&ED under subsection 248(1).

To help finance its growth, NovaVaxion has been offered a $4,000,000 conditionally repayable contribution from a federal regional development agency ("the Agency"). Under the draft Contribution Agreement, the $4,000,000 is described broadly as supporting "NovaVaxion's Thermostable Mucosal Vaccine Development and Commercialization Program," blending Initiatives A and B into a single global budget. Repayment under the draft contract is interest-free (0% interest), contingent upon NovaVaxion achieving commercial vaccine sales, calculated as a 5% royalty on gross revenues, and subject to a hard contractual sunset date in 2036 upon which any unpaid balance is extinguished. Internally, NovaVaxion tracks all employee time and laboratory consumables in a single general ledger R&D cost centre and files a single umbrella Form T661 project description covering the entire vaccine program.

Under the principles established in Immunovaccine (2014 FCA 196), this unedited structure creates an immediate disqualification trap. The $4,000,000 Agency contribution is unequivocally "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) due to its public-policy origin, revenue-contingent repayment, 2036 sunset clause, and zero interest rate. Furthermore, because the draft Contribution Agreement and NovaVaxion's internal project accounting commingle Initiative A (eligible SR&ED) and Initiative B (non-SR&ED), the CRA will determine that the $4,000,000 assistance was received "in respect of" the SR&ED claim under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18). Consequently, NovaVaxion's $4,000,000 of qualified SR&ED expenditures will be ground down to $0, destroying up to $1,400,000 in federal 35% enhanced RITCs alongside provincial R&D tax credits.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Blueprint
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance and Work Breakdown Structure (WBS)

Under subsection 127(18) of the ITA and section 2.0 of the CRA Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, government assistance reduces qualified SR&ED expenditures only to the extent that the assistance is "in respect of the SR&ED work performed in the year" on a specific project basis. NovaVaxion must immediately dismantle its monolithic program structure and establish two legally, technically, and administratively autonomous corporate projects approved by formal Board of Directors resolutions. The first project, designated Project SR&ED-101 (Self-Funded Experimental Development), must be restricted exclusively to resolving technological uncertainties in LNP lyophilization and mucosal adjuvant cross-linking. The second project, designated Project COMM-202 (Agency-Funded Commercialization & Clinical Regulatory Execution), must be restricted exclusively to non-SR&ED Phase I/II clinical trial management, Health Canada regulatory submissions, market access studies, and commercial packaging facility validation. Each project must be assigned a dedicated Project Charter, separate principal investigators, and mutually exclusive Work Breakdown Structure ("WBS") task codes so that no technical activity overlaps between the two governance streams.
Step 2: Restructuring Contract Terms and Financing Instruments

Before executing the funding agreement, NovaVaxion's legal counsel must execute a dual-pronged contractual remediation depending on whether the company retains the conditional contribution or transitions to a commercial loan facility. Under the first approach—contractual allocation and ring-fencing of the conditional contribution—if NovaVaxion retains the Agency's conditionally repayable contribution, counsel must amend the Contribution Agreement's Statement of Work (Schedule A) and Eligible Expenditure Budget (Schedule B) to stipulate explicitly that 100% of the Agency's $4,000,000 contribution is allocated exclusively to reimburse non-SR&ED commercialization, clinical trial, and regulatory costs under Project COMM-202. The contract must include an express negative covenant stating that no portion of the Agency contribution may be applied toward, or claimed against, experimental development wages, materials, or overhead incurred in Project SR&ED-101. Because the assistance is contractually and factually restricted to non-SR&ED expenditures, it is not "in respect of" SR&ED and cannot trigger the paragraph 37(1)(d) or subsection 127(18) grind against Project SR&ED-101.

Alternatively, under the second approach—conversion to a commercial debt facility satisfying CCLC Technologies—if any public-sector financing must be used to fund Project SR&ED-101 directly, NovaVaxion must reject the conditional contribution model and instead secure a commercial venture debt facility from a Crown financial institution operating with a commercial mandate (such as the Business Development Bank of Canada's commercial lending arm) structured to satisfy Immunovaccine and CCLC Technologies. To achieve this standard, the loan agreement must eliminate all revenue-contingent royalty clauses so that the principal constitutes an unconditional debt obligation payable on a fixed maturity schedule regardless of product sales. It must also remove the 2036 expiration and extinguishment clause, replacing it with standard commercial events of default and security registration under the Personal Property Security Act ("PPSA"). Finally, the facility must replace the 0% interest term with a market-benchmark interest rate (such as Prime +3.5% per annum) without multi-year interest-free deferrals, thereby proving that the lender acted to earn a commercial return on capital. Since the enactment of the "excluded loan" definition in subsection 12(11), a non-forgivable public-sector loan evidenced in writing, for which bona fide arrangements for repayment within a reasonable time are made when the loan is advanced and whose funds are used to earn income from a business, is excluded from "government assistance" even at a concessional interest rate; the market-rate terms therefore provide additional support for the loan's commercial character rather than a statutory requirement.
Step 3: Technical Documentation and Contemporaneous Experimentation Tracking

To defend the ring-fencing of Project SR&ED-101 during a CRA joint technical-financial audit, NovaVaxion must align its technical documentation with its contractual boundaries. When preparing its SR&ED claim, NovaVaxion must file Form T661 claiming solely the technological uncertainties, hypotheses, and systematic experimental iterations of Project SR&ED-101, while omitting all clinical trial protocols and cGMP scale-up descriptions belonging to Project COMM-202. In the laboratory, research personnel must maintain electronic laboratory notebooks ("ELNs") where every experimental run is tagged with the Project SR&ED-101 WBS code, recording the specific baseline formulation constraint, the formulated hypothesis, the analytical test results (such as dynamic light scattering particle size distributions), and the scientific conclusions. Simultaneously, NovaVaxion must require all scientists and technicians who split time between bench-scale LNP experimentation (Project SR&ED-101) and clinical trial batch QA/QC (Project COMM-202) to sign bi-weekly timesheets allocating exact daily hours by WBS task code. All Agency claim reimbursement certificates must attach only the timesheets and third-party vendor invoices bearing Project COMM-202 codes.
Step 4: Financial Tracking, Tax Reconciliation, and Subsection 127(10.7) Repayment Architecture

NovaVaxion's tax advisors must implement a rigorous accounting and tax reconciliation protocol across the T2 return. First, the accounting department must establish separate general ledger sub-accounts (Dept. 101 for SR&ED versus Dept. 202 for Agency-Funded Commercialization) so that no invoice or payroll journal entry is ever commingled. Second, this segregation protects the Prescribed Proxy Amount ("PPA"): under the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, government assistance reduces the SR&ED pool only if it relates to an expenditure claimed for SR&ED, and assistance that does not reimburse SR&ED salaries does not reduce the salary base used to compute the 55% PPA for overhead. By keeping 100% of Project SR&ED-101 salaries free of Agency assistance, NovaVaxion preserves both its direct salary base and its full PPA notional overhead addition for ITC calculation.

Third, NovaVaxion must manage the income tax treatment of the non-SR&ED assistance under paragraph 12(1)(x). Because the $4,000,000 Agency contribution allocated to Project COMM-202 does not reduce the subsection 37(1) SR&ED pool, it would ordinarily be included in income under paragraph 12(1)(x). NovaVaxion will offset this income inclusion dollar-for-dollar against the $4,000,000 of deductible current commercialization and clinical operating expenses incurred in Project COMM-202 (or file an election under subsection 12(2.2) to reduce the deductible non-SR&ED outlays directly), resulting in $0 net taxable income impact while leaving the $4,000,000 SR&ED claim completely intact. Fourth, as a fallback mechanism for any residual government assistance that does touch SR&ED expenditures, NovaVaxion must maintain a multi-year Government Assistance Repayment & ITC Recapture Schedule tracking annual gross-revenue royalty payments made to the Agency, ensuring that every dollar repaid is immediately added back to the deductible SR&ED pool under paragraph 37(1)(c) and claimed as ITC additions under paragraph (e.1) of the "investment tax credit" definition in subsection 127(9) and subsection 127(10.7) on Schedule T2SCH31.

body.text: Case Study 2: Aerospace and Clean-Hydrogen Propulsion Systems (Overcoming Public Authority Commercial Venture Deficiencies and Non-Arm's Length Assistance Allocation)
Factual Scenario and Initial Legal Pitfalls

AeroHydro Dynamics Corp. ("ParentCo") is a Canadian aerospace manufacturer based in Montreal, Quebec, and the 100% parent of AeroHydro Propulsion Labs Inc. ("SubCo"), a specialized R&D subsidiary in Ottawa, Ontario. ParentCo and SubCo are developing a next-generation liquid-hydrogen fuel cell turbine ("Project CryoThrust") for regional commuter aircraft. During the 2026 taxation year, the corporate group incurs $15,000,000 in project costs. SubCo incurs $10,000,000 in core SR&ED and specialized capital equipment, consisting of $8,000,000 in current wages, materials, and PPA overhead resolving cryogenic hydrogen embrittlement and fuel-cell membrane thermal runaway, plus $2,000,000 in new specialized cryogenic test-rig capital equipment eligible under the restored post-December 16, 2024 SR&ED capital expenditure rules enacted in S.C. 2026, c. 3. Meanwhile, ParentCo incurs $5,000,000 in commercial airframe integration and certification work, consisting of $2,000,000 in secondary integration SR&ED and $3,000,000 in routine commercial engineering for airframe nacelles manufacturing, Transport Canada airworthiness certification documentation, and commercial flight-simulator software packaging.

To fund Project CryoThrust, ParentCo enters into two public-sector agreements totaling $12,000,000. The first contract ("Agreement 1") is a $7,000,000 Strategic Industry Contribution Agreement with a federal industrial innovation department; while Agreement 1 requires unconditional repayment of principal over 15 years, it includes a five-year interest-free and principal-free grace period, a below-market concessional interest rate thereafter, no target commercial rate of return for the government, and broad socio-economic reporting covenants—terms comparable to the below-market, non-commercial loan found to be government assistance in CAE (the Immunovaccine Agreement, by contrast, was interest-free, repayable only as a percentage of gross income earned, and ended in 2017 whether or not repaid). The second contract ("Agreement 2") is a $5,000,000 co-development agreement with a provincial Crown regional aviation authority ("CrownAir") that operates northern commuter flights; CrownAir advances $5,000,000 to ParentCo to support Project CryoThrust in exchange for future discounted turbine maintenance and a conditional royalty capped at $5,000,000 expiring in 2034. ParentCo receives all $12,000,000 directly into its corporate bank account, transfers working capital to SubCo via intercompany advances, and fails to file prescribed Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) by its filing-due date.

This arrangement triggers two severe disqualification traps under Immunovaccine (2014 FCA 196) and CAE (2022 FCA 178). First, the $5,000,000 CrownAir advance will be classified as "government assistance" under subsection 127(9): it fails the CCLC Technologies test because CrownAir included a capped, zero-interest royalty expiring in 2034, and, being repayable only conditionally, it is not an "excluded loan" under subsection 12(11). The $7,000,000 industry advance has concessional terms comparable to the loan found to be government assistance in CAE, but because it is a non-forgivable loan requiring unconditional repayment of principal, it is excluded from the subsection 127(9) definition as an "excluded loan" if it is evidenced in writing, bona fide arrangements for its repayment within a reasonable time were made when it was advanced, and its funds are used to earn income from a business. If any of those conditions is not met, the $7,000,000 is also government assistance, bringing the total to $12,000,000. Second, the group suffers a cascading non-arm's length reduction and a paragraph 12(1)(x) income inclusion. Because ParentCo received $5,000,000 of assistance on Project CryoThrust (or $12,000,000 if Agreement 1 is not an excluded loan) while incurring only $2,000,000 of eligible SR&ED expenditures itself, ParentCo's $2,000,000 QEs are reduced to $0 under subsection 127(18), leaving $3,000,000 (or $10,000,000) of unapplied project assistance. Under subsection 127(19), because ParentCo and SubCo do not deal at arm's length, the unapplied excess assistance cascades onto SubCo, reducing SubCo's $10,000,000 QEs by $3,000,000 (or wiping them out entirely) while simultaneously exposing ParentCo to immediate corporate income inclusion under subparagraphs 12(1)(x)(iv) and 12(1)(v) on the excess over its subsection 37(1) pool.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Blueprint
Step 1: Restructuring Contract Terms to Satisfy the CCLC Technologies Commercial Venture Standard

To remove the $5,000,000 CrownAir transaction and the $7,000,000 financing from the scope of "government assistance" under subsection 127(9), counsel must restructure both agreements prior to execution to align with CCLC Technologies and Consumers' Gas. Under CCLC Technologies, payments by a public authority are not government assistance if made "in exactly the same way for exactly the same reasons as payments made by private business, that is, for the purpose of advancing the [business] interests of the payor". Because CrownAir operates a commercial regional airline fleet, counsel must redraft Agreement 2 from a "co-development subsidy" into a bilateral Commercial Fleet Supply and Joint-Venture Investment Agreement. Specifically, the contractual recitals and board minutes must document that CrownAir is entering into the transaction in its proprietary business capacity as a fleet operator to lower its aviation fuel costs and secure priority commercial delivery slots for 10 production turbines. Counsel must also eliminate the $5,000,000 return cap and the 2034 expiration clause, provisions analogous to those the FCA cited in Immunovaccine (an agreement ending in 2017 whether or not repaid, and a maximum recovery limited to the return of the contribution without interest). Instead, the $5,000,000 must be structured as a $3,000,000 advance commercial deposit for the delivery of production nacelles and commercial flight-simulator packages (non-SR&ED commercial goods) under ParentCo's $3,000,000 commercial manufacturing scope, paired with a $2,000,000 uncapped commercial royalty and equity participation bearing an internal rate of return ("IRR") hurdle of 14% modeled on private aerospace venture benchmarks.

Simultaneously, to prevent the $7,000,000 loan under Agreement 1 from being classified as government assistance under Immunovaccine and CAE, ParentCo must document that it qualifies as an "excluded loan" under subsection 12(11): a non-forgivable loan evidenced in writing, for which bona fide arrangements for repayment within a reasonable time are made when the loan is advanced, and whose funds are used to earn income from a business. The excluded-loan exception does not require a market interest rate, so the concessional rate and grace period do not by themselves make the loan government assistance, but any forgiveness or revenue-contingent repayment term would take it outside the exception. ParentCo must also explicitly allocate the loan proceeds in the Credit Agreement exclusively to finance commercial working capital, non-SR&ED certification, and non-SR&ED production tooling.
Step 2: Restructuring Multi-Entity Project Governance and Non-Arm's Length Assistance Allocations (Form T1145)

Where any residual government assistance or contract payment remains within a multi-entity corporate group, strict statutory compliance under subsections 127(19) and 127(20) is mandatory. First, ParentCo and SubCo must execute a formal Master Intercompany R&D Services Agreement clearly delineating SubCo's autonomous ownership and execution of the core cryogenic fuel-cell SR&ED (Project Cryo-SR&ED-01) versus ParentCo's execution of airframe certification and commercial customer integration (Project Cryo-COMM-02). Second, for any assistance that cannot be completely excluded from SR&ED, ParentCo (as transferor) and SubCo (as transferee) must execute and file prescribed Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) under subsection 127(20) on or before ParentCo's tax return filing-due date for the year. Where subsection 127(19) does not apply, filing Form T1145 under subsection 127(20) avoids subsection 127(21), which otherwise deems the unallocated excess to be government assistance received by the non-arm's length party.
Step 3: Technical Documentation and Experimental Segregation

To ensure the CRA cannot recharacterize the CrownAir commercial procurement payments as "contract payments for SR&ED to be performed for or on behalf of a Canadian public authority" under the subsection 127(9) definition of "contract payment", the technical documentation must establish a rigid firewall between commercial deliverables and experimental development. Under the CRA Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, a payment from a public authority is a "contract payment" grinding QEs under subsection 127(18) only if the contract requires SR&ED to be performed for or on behalf of the payer. Accordingly, the CrownAir contract Statement of Work must specify that CrownAir is contracting strictly for standard commercial airworthiness integration and finished commercial hardware deliverables from ParentCo, while SubCo performs its cryogenic fuel-cell SR&ED entirely on its own behalf and retains 100% legal and beneficial ownership of all foreground SR&ED intellectual property. In parallel, SubCo's engineering team must log all finite-element thermal modeling, cryogenic seal failure analyses, and bench-test iterations under SubCo's proprietary SR&ED project repository, completely divorced from ParentCo's customer deliverable milestone reports sent to CrownAir.
Step 4: Experimentation Costing, Capital Expenditure Restoration Rules, and Accrual Audit Defense

Finally, the corporate group must harmonize its tax costing schedules with current Canadian SR&ED legislation (including S.C. 2026, c. 3) and appellate evidentiary standards. Following the legislative restoration of SR&ED capital expenditures for property acquired on or after December 16, 2024 (enacted March 26, 2026 under S.C. 2026, c. 3), SubCo's $2,000,000 cryogenic test-rig acquisition qualifies for SR&ED deductions and ITCs. To prevent any public equipment subsidy from grinding the capital cost of the test rig under subsection 13(7.1) or subsection 127(18), SubCo must pay for 100% of the cryogenic test rig using internal equity funds traced through a dedicated capital bank account, while allocating any public industrial assistance strictly to ParentCo's non-SR&ED commercial manufacturing equipment—which is recorded on Schedule 8 net of subsection 13(7.1) assistance, thereby also excluding that amount from paragraph 12(1)(x) income.

Moreover, recognizing that the Tax Court's factual characterization of a funding agreement is insulated on appeal by the Housen v. Nikolaisen "palpable and overriding error" standard, tax counsel must assemble an audit-ready Commercial Venture Evidentiary File at the time the contracts are signed. This file must contain independent commercial valuation opinions, private-market interest rate term sheets, financial projections demonstrating the public counter-party's commercial IRR, and correspondence confirming the absence of public-policy forgiveness clauses—ensuring that if the Minister challenges the transaction, the taxpayer can conclusively satisfy the CCLC Technologies and Immunovaccine burden of proof at first instance before the Tax Court of Canada.
